description: How impact craters and meteorite finds inform interpretations of Earth and its biosphere.
content_html:
Craters as a Geological Tool

Every solid body in the Solar System that has a hard surface bears the scars of meteorite impacts. On the Moon and Mars, ancient craters survive for billions of years because those bodies lack the erosion and crustal recycling that erase them on Earth. On Earth, impacts have occurred throughout geological history — but most craters have been destroyed by weathering, burial, or subduction. Studying impact craters across the Solar System, and the rare well-preserved examples on Earth, reveals both the bombardment history of the inner Solar System and the profound effects that large impacts have had on the evolution of life.

Structure of an Impact Crater

When a meteorite or comet strikes a planetary surface at high velocity, it releases enormous energy in a fraction of a second. The impactor vaporises and the target rock melts, fractures and is thrown outward in all directions, forming a bowl-shaped impact crater. The key features of a typical impact crater, from largest to smallest, are:

  • The rim — a raised ring of uplifted and overturned rock surrounding the depression.
  • The ejecta blanket — a sheet of material thrown outward from the impact, covering the surrounding terrain to a depth that decreases with distance from the rim.
  • The crater floor — which may be filled with impact melt rock (solidified from the initially melted target rock) or, over time, with sediment.
  • A central peak (in larger craters) — a rebound structure formed as the initially depressed floor rebounded upward after the impact.
Key Fact

The four main features of an impact crater are: (1) the raised rim of uplifted rock; (2) the ejecta blanket of material thrown outward; (3) the crater floor, which may contain impact melt or sediment; and (4) a central peak (in large craters) formed by the elastic rebound of the crater floor. These features allow geologists to identify ancient craters even where erosion has partially degraded them.

Moon Craters and the Bombardment Record

The Moon’s surface records the full history of meteorite bombardment in the inner Solar System because it has no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics to erase craters over time. The lunar highlands — the pale, heavily cratered regions — preserve impact craters up to about 4 billion years old. The dark basaltic plains (the maria) have fewer craters because they were formed by volcanic eruptions between about 3.9 and 3.0 billion years ago, resurfacing and burying older craters.

By counting the number of craters of different sizes on a surface and applying crater counting, geologists can estimate the relative ages of different terrain units. Densely cratered regions are older; sparsely cratered regions are younger. On the Moon, the youngest recognisable features are small, fresh-looking craters with sharp rims and bright ejecta rays — features that fade over time as the surface is gardened by micrometeorites and space weathering.

Crater counting applies the principle of superposition at a planetary scale. If a small crater sits on top of an older, larger crater, the smaller one is younger. If a crater is itself heavily cratered and its rim is degraded, it is older than a nearby fresh crater with a sharp rim. This method allows geologists to build a relative time sequence for planetary surfaces without any radiometric dates — though Apollo lunar samples, radiocarbon-dated using radiometric methods, have calibrated the crater count chronology for the Moon, giving numerical ages to different crater-count densities.

Mars Craters and the Jezero Crater

Mars preserves impact craters ranging from tiny bowl-shaped depressions a few metres across to ancient multi-ring basins hundreds of kilometres in diameter. The most scientifically significant crater currently being studied is Jezero Crater, which is approximately 49 km wide. Orbital imagery reveals fan-shaped sedimentary deposits at the crater rim that are interpreted as river delta deposits — evidence that liquid water once flowed into the crater from outside, bringing sediment and potentially organic material. The Perseverance rover has been drilling rock cores from these deposits since 2021, searching for signs of past microbial life.

Jezero Crater illustrates how impact craters can function as natural traps for sediment, water and any materials carried in by rivers. On Earth, ancient impact craters that have been filled with sediment have sometimes produced economically important mineral deposits — the Sudbury Basin in Canada, for example, is a 1.85-billion-year-old impact structure that hosts one of the world’s largest nickel-copper ore deposits, thought to have formed when the impact melted and redistributed metal-rich rocks.

Key Fact

Jezero Crater on Mars is about 49 km across and contains sedimentary delta deposits at its rim, interpreted as the remains of an ancient river that flowed into the crater. NASA’s Perseverance rover landed there in February 2021 to drill cores from these deposits, which could preserve signs of ancient microbial life in the ancient lake sediments.

Impacts and the Evolution of Life on Earth

Large impacts have profoundly shaped Earth’s biosphere. The most famous example is the Chicxulub impact, which struck the Yucatan Peninsula (Mexico) about 66 million years ago. The impactor was roughly 10 km in diameter and released energy equivalent to billions of nuclear weapons. The immediate effects included wildfires, a global “impact winter” (dust and soot blocking sunlight for months to years), and the disruption of photosynthesis. The geological evidence for this event is a thin layer of iridium-enriched clay found at the Cretaceous–Palaeogene boundary in rocks worldwide. Iridium is far more abundant in meteorites than in Earth’s crust, so its global spike at this boundary is interpreted as fallout from the Chicxulub impactor.

The Chicxulub event caused the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, eliminating approximately 75% of all species, including all non-avian dinosaurs. Paradoxically, it also opened ecological opportunities for the surviving mammal lineages, allowing their diversification into the forms that eventually led to primates and humans. Large impacts, while catastrophic in the short term, are therefore part of the mechanism that shaped the trajectory of biological evolution on Earth.

Earth has been struck by at least as many meteorites as the Moon, but the geological record preserves very few confirmed impact structures compared to the lunar surface. This is because Earth has: (1) active weathering and erosion by water and wind, which gradually remove crater rims and infill depressions; (2) plate tectonics, which subducts old ocean floor (where many oceanic impacts would have occurred) and drives mountain building that deforms ancient terrains; (3) abundant vegetation that covers and masks topographic features. Only about 190 confirmed impact structures are known on Earth. The Moon, with no such processes, has hundreds of thousands of craters visible to telescopes. This contrast dramatically illustrates how active geological processes on Earth erase evidence of past events that are permanently readable on quieter planetary bodies.

Reading Planetary Surfaces: Connecting the Unit

Impact craters, like all geological features, are records of events in time. The youngest craters on any planetary surface are sharp-rimmed and show unmodified ejecta; the oldest are heavily degraded or buried. By reading these features, geologists construct relative timelines for planetary bodies — the same fundamental approach used in stratigraphy on Earth. Together, the lessons in this unit have traced Earth’s climate and Solar System history through rock evidence, ice cores, sea level change, atmospheric chemistry and planetary geology, demonstrating that the geological record — on Earth and beyond — is a rich archive waiting to be decoded.
exam_tip_html: When answering sequence questions about impact craters, work from oldest to youngest using superposition (features that are cross-cut or buried are older) and the state of preservation (degraded rims = older; sharp rims with bright ejecta rays = younger). For questions about the Chicxulub impact and mass extinction, mention the iridium layer as the chemical evidence — this is the geological ‘fingerprint’ of the impact in the rock record worldwide. Do not confuse the impact winter (short-term dust blocking sunlight) with longer-term climate change from CO2. For Jezero Crater, the key examiner point is that the delta deposits suggest ancient liquid water, making it a target for evidence of past life.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Impact craters have a characteristic structure (raised rim, ejecta blanket, crater floor, central peak in large craters) that allows identification even in degraded form; crater counting gives relative ages of planetary surfaces.
  • Jezero Crater on Mars (~49 km across) contains ancient river delta sediments and is the site of the Perseverance rover mission (landed February 2021), investigating whether ancient life existed in the lake that once filled the crater.
  • The Chicxulub impact (~66 million years ago) caused the end-Cretaceous mass extinction; its geological evidence is a global iridium-enriched clay layer at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, a chemical signature of extraterrestrial impact.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct geological evidence for the Chicxulub impact event at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary?
A) A layer of tillite widespread across Mexico
B) A global layer of iridium-enriched clay
C) A sequence of chalk formed in warm tropical seas
D) A worldwide unconformity with no clay layer
practice_questions.marks: B) A global layer of iridium-enriched clay [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Mars crater chosen as the landing site for the Perseverance rover and state the main geological reason for its selection.
practice_questions.marks: Jezero Crater — selected because it contains sedimentary delta deposits interpreted as an ancient river flowing into the crater, suggesting the presence of past liquid water (and potentially life) [1 mark for name; accept either part alone for 1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the main structural features of an impact crater.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: raised rim of uplifted rock / ejecta blanket of ejected material / crater floor (possibly with impact melt or sediment) / central peak in large craters (rebound structure). Two marks for two clearly described features. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Moon preserves ancient impact craters billions of years old, whereas Earth has very few ancient impact structures visible at the surface.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (1) The Moon has no atmosphere, so no wind or rain erosion to degrade crater rims and fill depressions; (2) the Moon has no plate tectonics, so ancient crust is not subducted or deformed — old craters remain where they formed; (3) Earth has active weathering, erosion by water, and plate tectonics (subduction of ocean floor, mountain building) that progressively destroy and bury impact structures. All three points with clear explanation.
Secure: Two correct processes on each body clearly contrasted.
Developing: Identifies erosion or tectonics as a reason for Earth but does not fully contrast with Moon.
Emerging: States that the Moon has more craters than Earth without explaining why. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A geologist examining satellite images of the Martian surface notices that one impact crater has a sharp, well-defined rim and bright ejecta rays extending outward, while a neighbouring crater has a degraded, rounded rim and no visible ejecta. Use the principle of superposition and the state of preservation to determine the relative ages of the two craters.
practice_questions.marks: Full marks require: (1) correctly identifying the sharp-rimmed, bright-rayed crater as the younger feature and the degraded, rounded crater as the older; (2) applying superposition: older features are modified by later processes — the rounded rim has been subjected to longer exposure to space weathering and micrometeorite gardening; (3) explaining that ejecta rays fade over time as the surface is gardened, so their presence indicates youth; (4) linking to the broader principle that the least modified surface feature is youngest. [4 marks: 1 per point; maximum 4]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how evidence from impact craters on the Moon and Mars has improved our understanding of the early geological and biological history of Earth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Craters on the Moon (no erosion or recycling) give a complete bombardment record going back 4 billion years; applied to Earth via crater counting calibration using Apollo samples, this shows early Earth was intensely bombarded during the Hadean (4.6–4.0 Ga), a period almost absent from Earth's own rock record. Jezero Crater on Mars illustrates how craters trap sediment and water — river deltas inside craters preserve ancient environmental conditions including potentially biological material; the search for biosignatures there informs understanding of life's origin on Earth. The Chicxulub impact shows that large impacts reset biospheres — studying impact geology therefore informs the major extinction events in Earth's history. Evaluates the limits: planetary analogy has limits (different gravity, atmosphere, and tectonic context); absence of Mars/Moon fossils means biological conclusions are still speculative. Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
Secure: Addresses at least two contributions to Earth understanding with specific examples; one limitation discussed; conclusion present.
Developing: Describes what can be learnt without clearly evaluating or reaching a conclusion.
Emerging: Makes simple points about craters or impacts without linking to Earth understanding. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the geological evidence for the Chicxulub impact found in rocks worldwide?
options: A layer of tillite with angular clasts
A global layer of iridium-enriched clay at the K-Pg boundary
An unconformity showing a gap in sedimentation
A layer of chalk indicating warm seas

knowledge_checks.q: On a planetary surface with no resurfacing, which feature indicates the youngest surface unit?
options: Heavily cratered terrain with degraded rims
A crater with bright ejecta rays and a sharp rim
A multi-ring basin hundreds of kilometres wide
A region covered by ancient anorthosite

knowledge_checks.q: The technique of estimating the age of a planetary surface by counting the number of impact craters per unit area is called _____ counting.
Jezero Crater was selected as the Perseverance rover landing site because it contains _____ deposits that suggest ancient liquid water once flowed into the crater.
Match each crater-related term to its correct description:
right: Sheet of material thrown outward from an impact, covering the surrounding terrain
Rebound structure formed at the centre of large craters as the floor springs back upward
Global chemical evidence for extraterrestrial impact, concentrated in meteorites not Earth's crust

flashcard_questions.a: A circular depression formed by a hypervelocity meteorite or comet strike, with a raised rim and ejecta blanket.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the ejecta blanket of an impact crater?
flashcard_questions.a: Material thrown outward from the impact, covering surrounding terrain to a depth that decreases with distance.

flashcard_questions.q: In which rock layer is the global evidence for the Chicxulub impact found?
flashcard_questions.a: An iridium-enriched clay layer at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, about 66 million years ago.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is iridium useful as evidence for a meteorite impact?
flashcard_questions.a: It is very rare in Earth's crust but concentrated in meteorites, so a global iridium spike indicates extraterrestrial fallout.

flashcard_questions.q: What mass extinction did the Chicxulub impact trigger?
flashcard_questions.a: The end-Cretaceous mass extinction, eliminating about 75% of species including non-avian dinosaurs.

flashcard_questions.q: What is crater counting and what does it reveal?
flashcard_questions.a: Counting craters per unit area to estimate relative surface age — more craters means an older surface.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a crater with a sharp rim and bright ejecta rays indicate a young age?
flashcard_questions.a: Ejecta rays fade and rims are rounded over time by space weathering — their preservation indicates recent formation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Jezero Crater and why is it geologically significant?
flashcard_questions.a: A 49 km Mars crater with ancient river delta deposits, chosen as the Perseverance rover landing site for biosignature research.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the central peak of a large impact crater?
flashcard_questions.a: A rebound structure at the crater centre, formed as the initially depressed floor springs elastically upward after impact.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Earth have fewer visible impact craters than the Moon?
flashcard_questions.a: Erosion, weathering and plate tectonics destroy and bury craters — only about 190 confirmed structures are known on Earth.

flashcard_questions.q: How did the Chicxulub impact affect biological evolution in the long term?
flashcard_questions.a: It opened ecological niches for mammals by wiping out the non-avian dinosaurs, enabling mammal diversification.

glossary_terms.definition: A circular depression on a planetary surface formed by the hypervelocity impact of a meteorite or comet, characterised by a raised rim, ejecta blanket and, in larger craters, a central peak.
The technique of estimating the relative or absolute age of a planetary surface by counting the density of impact craters: older surfaces have more craters per unit area than younger resurfaced ones.

A principle of relative dating stating that older geological features are progressively buried or modified by younger ones; applied to planetary surfaces, impact craters formed on older terrain will themselves be cratered by later impacts.

An ancient impact crater on Mars, about 49 km in diameter, chosen as the landing site for NASA's Perseverance rover because it contains sedimentary deposits interpreted as the delta of an ancient river that flowed into the crater.

A large meteorite impact approximately 66 million years ago, recorded by a layer of iridium-enriched clay at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, linked to the mass extinction that ended the reign of non-avian dinosaurs.
A chemical element extremely rare in Earth's crust but concentrated in meteorites, used as a chemical marker for extraterrestrial impact events in the rock record.
